To be clear: Big picture: Buying / selling real estate in the US is better than most any other country in the world. The odds of you getting screwed through major fraud are close to zero. I have VERY high confidence in the US law system with respect to property ownership, transfer, and overall rights. (This is NOT the case in most other countries outside the Western Europe, Japan, Canada, etc.) The state laws and the law firms that create the contracts, etc. are all very good. Major fraud isn't what you should worry about. What you have to worry about with a real estate agent is the smaller / soft things.

Such as:

- Which school district the house is in. (If you don't have it in writing, it doesn't exist.)

- How much it will cost to remodel the kitchen, foundation repair, etc. (They have bias, depending if you are buying or selling.)

- How much house can you afford on your budget. (They are not financial advisors.)

- How the neighborhood is "up and coming" or whatever.

- About the HOA, about the city "feel", etc.

- What house is best for you and your family. (Fun to pretend to be interested in a property then watch them try to push it on you.)

- About the tax rates, about the utility expenses are.

- What a house should be bought / sold for. (They have bias, depending if you are buying or selling.)

Bottom line: If you get something in writing, then you can trust it. If it is just verbal from the real estate agent, then it may or may not be true and accurate.

One final point: ALWAYS get a house inspected before you buy it. (Best $$ spent.) But, NEVER EVER EVER use the one the real estate agent recommends. Basic conflict of interest: If a home inspector makes most of his money from real estate agent referrals, then he will have a false insensitive to be "soft" on his inspections. If he is "hard" on inspections and finds lots of problems, then the real estate agent will stop recommending his services and go with another home inspector who will be "soft". See the conflict of interest? Even if the agent is perfectly ethical, you have to be careful with the home inspector who depends on the referrals. In this relationship, you are at a major disadvantage - you will only use the inspector's services once. But - that inspector needs a constant flow of new clients, mostly from real estate agent referrals.

Good luck!
